meaning.text: As a substantive, likho conveys the idea of something malevolent or unfortunate.
The adjective likhoi has two opposite meanings: sometimes what is evil, hurtful or malicious, sometimes what is bold and vigorous.
The Polish licho properly signifies uneven.
In the tales the name is rendered as evil: the smith sets out to seek evil (likho), and the Little-Russian story says 'This was Likho (Evil)'.

peoples_regions.region: Little-Russian (variant of the tale quoted by Afanasief)
South Russia (a proverb common to Poland and South Russia)

appearance_forms.label: One-eyed woman of the Voroneje tale (Ralston, Afanasyev)
Afanasyev's one-eyed giant of other variants

appearance.text: In the tale from the Voroneje Government, Likho takes a female form.
Afanasyev's retelling calls her a giantess.
In other variants of the tale Likho is represented as a giant.
This giant is taller than the tallest oak.
This giant has a single eye in the forehead.
A tale tells of a man who sought Likho, and it appeared to him in the shape of a one-eyed giant.

scene.text: In the Voroneje tale Likho is met in a dark, dense forest, reached along a small, narrow path.
Its dwelling is a large cottage standing in the forest.
The cottage is empty when the travellers enter, and everything looks bare and squalid.
The travellers come upon it at night.

appearance.text: The giant lies stretched out with his head in the corner (pokut) and his feet on the stove.

behavior_habitat.text: Likho lives in an iron castle standing beside a wood.
The castle is surrounded by a palisade of human bones tipped with skulls.
Likho lies on a couch of human bones.
Around Likho sit Zluidni (Woes) and Zhurba (Care).
A voice from the castle answers the seeker that evil is here.
Likho offers the guest a human head to eat.
Likho intends to eat the visitor.
When the guest flees, Likho hears the iron doors creak and cries to them to hold the fugitive.
The door slams on the fugitive's right hand and he loses it.
Some of the skazkas offer a personification of evil called Likho, somewhat resembling their picture of the supernatural witch.
To Likho is always attributed a character of unmitigated malevolence.
Among the Polish peasantry Licho describes an evil spirit, a sort of devil.
In the Voroneje tale Likho greets the travellers who come to spend the night and says she shall have something to sup on.
She lights the stove, cuts the tailor's throat, puts him in the oven and eats him.
She keeps a flock of sheep, drives them into her cottage for the night and lets them out in the morning one at a time, catching each by the wool on its back.
After she is blinded she sits down at the threshold of the cottage.
A golden-handled hatchet sticks in a tree in her forest, and the hand of the man who seizes it sticks fast to it.
She comes after the escaping smith, crying that he has not got away yet.
In other variants the giant Likho drives the sheep into the fold with a pine log.
Machal names the evil Dolya, the fate a man gets for his share, Nedolya or Licho.
For the man who gets an evil Dolya, all his toil and all his endeavours are of no avail.
The evil Dolya does nothing but sleep, dress herself or make merry, never offering him any aid.
A proverb says misfortune (likho) walks not through the trees but among people.
A proverb says: do not seek likho, it will find you itself.

dealing_with_it.text: A proverb common to Poland and South Russia says: When Likho sleeps, awake it not.
In the Voroneje tale the smith offers to forge her a new eye, ties her with a thick cord and puts out her sound eye with a red-hot awl.
He escapes by turning his sheepskin coat wool outward and crawling out among her sheep.
Caught by the hand on the golden-handled hatchet, he cuts off his own hand and so escapes.
In the Little-Russian variant the guest hides the human head Likho offers him instead of eating it, first under the bench and then in his bosom.

notes.text: origin: no source says where Likho comes from or who becomes one; searched likho, licho, one-eyed, лихо, лиха, лихомъ, одноглаз, лихо одноглаз and woe across all sources, and read ralston1873 pp.178-185, afanasyev1868 pp.696-700, afanasyev1869 pp.396-397 and machal1918 pp.251-252.

People terms not in sources/peoples.json, so no people row was written for them: 'На Руси' (afanasyev1868:p.698, where the tale of One-eyed Likho is introduced; proposed Russians); 'великорусской сказкѣ' (afanasyev1868:p.700, the Great-Russian tale; proposed Russians); 'малорусскій варіантъ' (afanasyev1868:p.699; proposed Ukrainians, as the table lists Малороссія but not the adjective); 'Voroneje Government' (ralston1873:p.178 footnote, where the tale comes from; proposed Russians). Because only these unlisted terms attach a people to the Cyrillic form, the printed forms 'Лихо' (afanasyev1868:pp.698-699) and 'Лихо одноглазое' (afanasyev1868:p.698) are not recorded as native rows, and Ralston's title 'One-eyed Likho' (ralston1873:p.178) is not recorded as a name variant.

Table rows matched by word form rather than exact term: Ralston's 'Little-Russian variant' (ralston1873:p.181) to the 'Little-Russians' row, and 'South Russia' (ralston1873:p.178) to the contested 'South-Russian' row (listed there for ralston1872). Both are recorded as Ukrainians.

The one-eyed giant of afanasyev1869:p.396 comes from a footnote that cites the same tale number (N. R. Sk. III, 14) that ralston1873:p.178 and afanasyev1868:p.698 tell with a one-eyed woman; the footnote calls it a giant, so it is filed under the giant form. Gore or Woe (ralston1873:pp.184-185) and Бѣда (afanasyev1869:pp.396-397) are separate personifications of misfortune and were not merged into Likho; only proverbs that print лихо were used.
